description: We are developing a NASA-data prototype to compare lunar landing sites and dates under landing dispersion and arrival delays. Our focus is transparent geometry, illumination, Earth visibility and electrical margins, with reproducible numerical checks.
summary: Three lunar south-pole sites meet the same power and visibility requirements if a lander arrives exactly on target and on time. Which site deserves a closer look if touchdown shifts or slips by a day? LIMEN lets student mission-design teams explore that decision using NASA lunar terrain and JPL ephemerides. Choose a site and date, inspect a failed landing, then change the battery and replay the same trajectory. In our 72-hour example, extra storage clears every sampled energy failure at the connecting ridge. Some arrivals still miss the Earth-visibility requirement. On another date, sunlight from the exposed edge of the solar disk changes whether the battery passes. The tool shows which constraint drives the decision, how sensitive the comparison is to sampling, and which assumptions another team would need to reproduce it.
details:
We built a browser-based prototype for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. A mission-design class can use it to decide whether to investigate a different site, reconsider the landing window or study a change in power storage. Start with the connecting ridge, de Gerlache area and Malapert area on 21 November 2026 at 00:00 UTC. Give each nominal landing the same 72-hour mission, 60 W load, one-square-metre solar panel and 2.4 kWh battery. All three start at 80% charge and stay at least 1,680 Wh above a 10% floor. That shared starting margin alone gives the team little basis for choosing among them.

NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter elevation grids let us reconstruct the terrain skyline at each sampled position. JPL Horizons supplies the local directions of the Sun and Earth through time. We calculate how much of the solar disk clears the skyline, integrate electrical generation and consumption, and track how long the centre of Earth remains visible. Battery capacity, required Earth-visible time and maximum blackout duration are adjustable; this example uses a fixed 10% battery floor.

In the 100 m comparison, each site contributes 121 landing positions and nine arrival times. Across 3,267 trajectories, we assign weights using an assumed 150 m landing dispersion and a uniform delay of up to 24 hours. The share of total model weight meeting both requirements is 73.87% at the connecting ridge, 86.33% at de Gerlache and 99.83% at Malapert. About 0.17% of the assumed spatial weight lies outside the sampled area. These figures describe the chosen scenarios. Their relationship to actual mission success has not been calibrated.

In the app’s 100 m ridge comparison, inspect a landing 200 m west of the target and 15 hours late. It reaches the electrical floor after about 26.6 hours. Apply 6.51 kWh and replay that same landing. It finishes with about 661 Wh, just above its new 651 Wh floor. Across the 100 m ridge ensemble, the larger battery clears the energy requirement in every sampled case. About 0.95% of model weight still misses geometric Earth visibility. The team can now investigate a different window for that constraint. A shareable link preserves the selected position, arrival and assumptions, and a CSV records the site comparison.

On 24 November at the nominal ridge point, the Sun’s centre stays below the skyline at all 432 ten-minute sample midpoints. A point-source model predicts zero generation and crosses the battery floor after 49.875 hours. Accounting for the visible part of the solar disk, with linear limb-darkening coefficient u = 0.56, gives 1,879.76 Wh of solar electricity and a minimum margin of 507.47 Wh above the 450 Wh floor. Both calculations use a 72-hour mission, 4.5 kWh battery at 80% initial charge, 60 W load, 1 m² vertical azimuth-tracking panel, and zero landing dispersion and delay. Halving both the skyline angle spacing and integration step gives a 507.58 Wh margin.

Moon Trek, QuickMap and MMGIS already support planetary exploration and planning. Fincannon studied illumination and electrical storage at the lunar south pole. Barker and colleagues studied how terrain uncertainty affects illumination estimates. Our contribution connects a site comparison, the cause of a specific failure and a reproducible battery experiment in one interface. Independent numerical checks cover partial solar occultation, battery accounting and the storage boundary. Refining the landing grid from 200 m to 100 m changed the de Gerlache score by 10.75 percentage points. A separate 50 m audit of the same 21 November footprint preserved the site ordering. With 2.4 kWh, the finer scores were 74.02% at the ridge, 86.49% at de Gerlache and 99.83% at Malapert. The largest change from 100 m was 0.16 percentage points. With 6.51 kWh, the ridge score fell from 98.88% on the 100 m grid to 97.33% on the 50 m grid, a 1.55-point change. Both samples cleared the electrical requirement, while the weight failing visibility rose from 0.95% to 2.50%. At de Gerlache, the same storage test rose from 93.41% to 94.61%. Agreement depends on the settings, and neither grid resolves every possible landing point.

The study covers three fixed locations and an archived date range. Unresolved relief between samples, thermal effects, landing hazards, station-specific radio links and battery mass would all matter to an operational decision. We provide source identifiers, archived ephemeris queries, model assumptions, numerical checks and research references so other teams can examine those limits.

Andrea Galesso and Camilla Galesso, Lunar Margin Lab, directed the project and are responsible for review and submission. OpenAI Codex assisted with implementation, data processing, numerical checks, debugging, writing and presentation preparation. ChatGPT image generation produced a conceptual lander illustration for the presentation. The scientific results come from the documented NASA inputs and numerical model.
